claims.text: Atomic-size misfit and stacking-fault energy primarily govern mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The investigated quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after controlled thermomechanical treatment.
Changing the relative concentrations of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni will systematically alter both average atomic-size misfit and stacking-fault energy.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes produce severe local lattice distortion and heterogeneous dislocation behavior.
Changes in stacking-fault width or partial-dislocation separation affect dislocation behavior.
Greater atomic-size misfit enhances lattice resistance to dislocation glide and increases solid-solution strengthening.
Stacking-fault energy controls Shockley-partial separation, dislocation mobility, and cross-slip.
The combined effects of atomic-size misfit and stacking-fault energy raise CRSS, yield strength, and hardness while potentially reducing ductility.
The equiatomic quinary baseline has a room-temperature CRSS of approximately 33–43 MPa.
Relative to the equiatomic baseline, alloys with greater atomic-size misfit and lower stacking-fault energy will have higher yield strength and hardness.
Alloys with lower atomic-size misfit will have lower strength and potentially greater ductility.
Lower stacking-fault energy will produce wider partial-dislocation separations and more pronounced obstacles to slip.
Short-range order can slightly increase yield strength without fundamentally changing activation of the plastic mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys under comparable thermomechanical processing and room-temperature or moderate-strain-rate testing.
At extreme temperatures or in non-FCC or multiphase alloys, phase transformations or twinning-induced plasticity may dominate the response.
The exact quantitative contributions of atomic-size misfit and stacking-fault energy remain uncertain and may be obscured by short-range order or other microstructural factors.
